classification.classification_note: Duplicate-username cleanup deletes the second inserted client but frees the first inserted client while it is still `data->clients`, so the next username lookup reads through a dangling hash head.

bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json issue description / sanitizer_trace.txt / reproduction_report.json / patch.diff / staged PoC / vulnerable source read from gt-arvo_58108-workspace
bug_description.normalized: The staged witness is the exact JSON file `{"clients":[{"username":"d"},{"username":"d"}]}`. After the dynamic-security plugin reads and parses that file, `dynsec_clients__config_load()` admits both client objects because both `username` fields are non-empty strings. It allocates and inserts the first duplicate client (`client1`), then allocates a distinct second duplicate (`client2`) and executes the same `HASH_ADD(hh, data->clients, username, username_len, client)` again without first checking `dynsec_clients__find(data, username)`. uthash appends `client2` after `client1` in app order but prepends it in bucket order, and the later `HASH_SORT(data->clients, client_cmp)` preserves insertion order for equal usernames, so cleanup still iterates `client1` first while username lookups for `"d"` return `client2`. During `mosquitto_plugin_cleanup()`, `HASH_ITER` saves `client_tmp = client2` before `client__free_item(data, client1)` runs. That free routine looks up by username, deletes `client2`, then frees `client1`, leaving `data->clients` itself dangling to freed `client1`. The loop then advances to the saved `client2`, and the next `dynsec_clients__find(data, client2->username)` dereferences the dangling head pointer in `HASH_FIND`, producing the observed AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free read at `plugins/dynamic-security/clients.c:70`. The fix closes the path by skipping a config entry when `dynsec_clients__find(data, username)` already reports an existing username before insertion.

source.description: First project-side read of the vulnerability-relevant input. This block extracts a client username from the attacker-controlled JSON object and accepts it for insertion only when it is a non-empty string.
source.value_from: The staged PoC is exactly `{"clients":[{"username":"d"},{"username":"d"}]}`. On both relevant loop iterations, `jtmp->valuestring` is `"d"` and `username_len` becomes `1`, so the same username value is admitted twice.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

sink.description: ASan crash site. On the second cleanup iteration, a username lookup dereferences the dangling `data->clients` head pointer left when the first inserted duplicate was freed without being removed from the hash.
sink.note: The saved ASan trace reports `READ of size 8` at `plugins/dynamic-security/clients.c:70:3` in `dynsec_clients__find`, called from `client__free_item()` line 81 during cleanup.

root_cause.description: Missing uniqueness check. The second `HASH_ADD` inserts a distinct `client2` with the same username as existing `client1`, creating the duplicate-key state that lets cleanup delete `client2` by name while later freeing `client1` in place.
root_cause.note: The fixing hunk adds `if(dynsec_clients__find(data, username)){ continue; }` before allocation/insertion so the second `"d"` client from the PoC is skipped instead of being added.

tainted_value_origin.description: Both vulnerability-relevant client objects in the witness contribute the same admitted username `"d"`, which becomes the duplicate hash key that drives the stale-entry cleanup path.

parser_admitted.description: The file has already parsed as JSON and reaches `dynsec_clients__config_load(data, tree)`, so the top-level `clients` array from the witness is handed to the vulnerable client loader instead of being rejected earlier.

fine_trace.note: Source. This parser block reads each client object's `username` from the attacker-controlled JSON tree and admits it only if it is a non-empty string. In the exact staged witness, both relevant `clients` elements yield the same admitted username `"d"` with `username_len == 1`.

On the first admitted `{"username":"d"}` object, the loader allocates the first duplicate client (`client1`) and copies `"d"` into its flexible `username` field. ASan's allocation stack identifies this line as the allocator for the later-freed 258-byte region.
The first insertion places `client1` into `data->clients` under username key `"d"`, making it both the app-order head and the bucket head before any duplicate exists.
On the second admitted `{"username":"d"}` object, the loader allocates a distinct second duplicate client (`client2`) and copies the same username `"d"` into it.

Root cause. Vulnerable code inserts `client2` even though `client1` already uses the same key `"d"`. uthash appends `client2` after `client1` in app order but prepends it to the hash bucket, so duplicate-key lookups by username now return `client2` first while `data->clients` still points to `client1`.

After loading all clients, `HASH_SORT(data->clients, client_cmp)` reorders the app-order list by `strcmp(username)`. Because `client_cmp` returns 0 for `client1` and `client2`, uthash's stable merge step keeps their insertion order, so app-order head remains `client1` while the bucket order from step 5 still makes `dynsec_clients__find(data, "d")` return `client2`.

The fuzz target always calls `mosquitto_plugin_cleanup()` after `mosquitto_plugin_init()`, and cleanup enters this loop to free every client in app order. `HASH_ITER` saves the next pointer before the body, so the first iteration sets `client = client1` from the app-order head and pre-saves `client_tmp = client2`.

While freeing `client1`, the code recovers a deletion target by username instead of by pointer. `HASH_FIND` searches the `"d"` bucket from its bucket head, so this lookup returns `client2`, not the current `client1` selected by step 7.

The `if(client_found)` branch is taken for `client2`, so `HASH_DEL(data->clients, client_found)` removes `client2` from the hash. Because `client2` has `hh.prev == client1`, uthash updates `client1->next` but does not replace the head pointer, so `data->clients` still equals `client1`; the `client_tmp` saved in step 7 still points to the unfreed `client2` object.

Cleanup then frees the current `client1` itself. Since step 9 deleted `client2` instead, `client1`'s hash entry was never removed, so `data->clients` becomes a dangling head pointer to freed memory. After the loop body, `HASH_ITER` advances to the saved `client_tmp` and starts a second iteration on `client2`.

Sink. On the next cleanup iteration, `client__free_item(data, client2)` immediately calls `dynsec_clients__find(data, client2->username)` at line 81. `HASH_FIND` uses the dangling head pointer `data->clients == client1`, so it dereferences freed `struct dynsec__client` state and triggers the observed heap-use-after-free read at line 70.

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: allocation_context at clients.c:141 is the first duplicate client's allocation site; the actual root cause is the later duplicate-key insertion at clients.c:240, and the trace links that allocation into the dangling-head cleanup path.

format.name: Mosquitto dynamic-security config JSON
format.contract: The verified trigger is the exact staged JSON `{"clients":[{"username":"d"},{"username":"d"}]}`. Its top-level `clients` array contributes exactly two admitted non-empty usernames, both equal to `"d"`, so `dynsec_clients__config_load()` allocates both duplicates and inserts both duplicate keys before cleanup. Stage 01 preserved only this witness; this contract does not generalize beyond inputs that preserve the same duplicate admitted-username state.

evidence_limitations: Stage 01 preserved only the vulnerable AddressSanitizer reproduction. Stage 02 did not execute a fixed build or a second detector, so `patch_resolves: true` remains source-grounded from `patch.diff` rather than dynamic differential validation.
